emails.subject: Start with one part of the business
emails.preheader: Choose the customer-process problem you most want to improve.
body: Welcome to the 30-day series. I’ll send you one practical idea or tool each day, along with ways The LeadFlow Pro can help.
Start here: finish this sentence.
“The part of our customer process I most want to improve is _____.”
It might be answering inquiries, explaining tuition, following up after an event or keeping track of coaching conversations. Choose the part that creates the most confusion for your team.
Reply with your answer. A clear starting point makes the next conversation more useful.

emails.subject: Try your website on your phone
emails.preheader: Check what a first-time visitor can understand and do.
body: Open your website on your phone and pretend you have never seen the business before.
Can you understand what is offered? Can you find the next step? Does the contact button work?
Our free Website Scorecard gives you a structured checklist to work through. It is a review of the answers you provide, not a prediction of leads or sales.
Choose one useful improvement from the list before trying to change everything.

emails.subject: Three answers your offer needs
emails.preheader: Make the audience, scope and next step easier to understand.
body: A prospective customer should not have to guess whether an offer fits.
Read your main page and look for three answers: who the offer serves, what is included and how to take the next step.

For a school, that might mean the program, format and inquiry process. For a coach, it might mean the problem addressed and how to discuss fit. For an event, it means the audience, topic and registration.
Write the missing answer in plain language today.

cta.label: Reply with the offer you want to clarify

emails.subject: What does a missed caller hear?
emails.preheader: A realistic voicemail greeting gives the caller a next step.
body: Your voicemail is part of the customer experience.
Listen to it. Does it identify the business? Explain what information to leave? Set an expectation your team can keep?
A useful greeting gives someone a reason to leave a clear message. Avoid promising an immediate callback if nobody is available to make it.
Our free script tool can help you draft a greeting. Read it aloud and adjust it to sound like you before using it.

emails.subject: Make the first reply useful
emails.preheader: Answer the question, then explain one next step.
body: An acknowledgment is a start. A helpful answer goes further.
Try this structure: thank the person, respond to the question they actually asked, then explain one next step.
“You asked about our evening program. Here is how that schedule works. Would a call or a visit help you decide whether it fits?”
Keep the details accurate. Avoid dropping someone into a generic sales pitch when they have asked a specific question.
Save a good example where your team can find it.

cta.label: Reply with a common customer question

emails.subject: Give the next step an owner
emails.preheader: Make one open inquiry easier for your team to handle.
body: Look at one open inquiry today.
Can you identify the person responsible, the next action and when that action should happen?
“We should follow up” is easy to lose in a busy day. “Jordan will answer the schedule question Tuesday morning” gives the team something concrete to do.
The tool matters less than whether your team can find and use the information. Start with a shared place and a clear responsibility.

cta.label: Tell Ryan which handoff needs an owner

emails.subject: Review one real customer journey
emails.preheader: Find a practical improvement by following one inquiry.
body: Take one inquiry from the past week and follow its path.
Where did it begin? Who saw it first? What answer did the person receive? What happened next?
You are looking for the handoff that needs attention. A missing reply, unclear form or forgotten appointment can point to a practical improvement.
Keep the review small enough to finish. One carefully understood conversation can tell you more than a long list of guesses.

cta.label: Reply with the handoff that needs work

emails.subject: Give your links useful names
emails.preheader: Consistent campaign labels help you review traffic.
body: When several posts point to the same page, it can be difficult to tell which one brought a visitor.
Campaign tags help you distinguish the links in your analytics. Our free UTM Link Builder lets you label the source, channel and campaign.
Use a consistent naming pattern your team understands. A tagged visit still is not a sale; connect it to later activity before drawing conclusions.
Start by labeling the next link you publish.

emails.subject: Put assumptions beside the ad budget
emails.preheader: Use your own numbers and label estimates honestly.
body: Before choosing a budget, write down the assumptions behind it.
How many inquiries do you hope to handle? What might each inquiry cost? How many become real customers in your own records?
The Ad Budget Planner helps you work through a scenario. Its output depends on your inputs; it is not a forecast or a promise.
If you do not know a number yet, label it as an estimate and replace it when your campaign produces evidence.

emails.subject: School owners: separate the questions
emails.preheader: Give tuition and funding questions an accurate next step.
body: Tuition questions and funding questions do not always have the same next step.
Make a short list of the payment options your school actually offers or accepts. Then note who can answer each question and what information the prospective student needs next.
Keep that explanation consistent across your page, form and follow-up.
Eligibility and approval belong to the applicable funding program and the individual’s circumstances. A clearer process helps your team explain what is known without promising an outcome.

emails.subject: Explain tuition before asking for a decision
emails.preheader: Make costs, inclusions and actual payment terms clear.
body: For a private-pay program, people may need to understand the cost before they are ready to talk about enrollment.
Check whether your information explains what is included, what is separate and when payments are due. If plans are available, describe only the terms you actually offer.
Clarity helps the conversation. It also gives your team a consistent reference when someone asks the same question in a different way.
Choose one tuition question and improve its answer today.

cta.label: Ask Ryan about your tuition explanation

emails.subject: Give your event invitation a clear job
emails.preheader: Help someone decide whether to attend and how to register.
body: A useful event invitation answers a few basic questions.
Who should attend? What will the session cover? When and where will it happen? What does registration involve?
Read your invitation without assuming the reader knows you. If the next step is difficult to find, make it easier to see.
For a virtual event, also check whether the time zone and joining instructions are clear. Small details deserve attention before you send more people to the page.

cta.label: Reply with the event you are planning

emails.subject: Put the appointment on the calendar
emails.preheader: Check the time zone and joining details before sharing.
body: After someone registers or chooses a time, make it easy to remember the details.
Our Add-to-Calendar Link Maker can create a calendar link for a class, consultation, open house or virtual event.
Check the time zone, location and joining link before sharing it. A calendar entry should agree with the confirmation message and event page.
Try the finished link yourself. That quick check can catch an avoidable source of confusion.

emails.subject: Make the mastermind fit easier to assess
emails.preheader: Explain participation and support before someone joins.
body: Someone considering a mastermind may need more than a list of meeting dates.
Explain who the group is for, how participation works and what is expected between sessions. Be specific about the support you actually provide.
Then give interested people a useful next step: ask a question, discuss fit or review the details.
Clear expectations help both sides decide whether the offer belongs in their plans. What question would someone need answered before joining yours?

cta.label: Reply with the question people ask

emails.subject: What happens after someone joins?
emails.preheader: Make the first useful community action easy to find.
body: For a community, the first useful experience matters.
Look at the welcome process. Can a new member find where to begin, introduce themselves and ask for help? Do they understand what the community offers?
You do not need a long introduction to explain those things. A short welcome with a clear first action can be easier to use.
Write the message from the perspective of someone opening the community for the first time.

cta.label: Tell Ryan about your welcome process

emails.subject: Know who owns the accounts
emails.preheader: Make ownership and access part of the project conversation.
body: Make a simple list of the accounts your business relies on: website, domain, advertising, email and customer records.
For each one, confirm who owns it and who can manage access.
The goal is a clear handoff and fewer surprises when someone’s role changes. Store access securely; do not put passwords into a shared planning document.
Our work is built around client-owned accounts and data. Ownership should be part of the project conversation from the beginning.

emails.subject: Ask what a result actually counts
emails.preheader: Read the definition, period and source behind a number.
body: A screenshot can look impressive without answering the question that matters to your business.
When you review marketing results, ask what was counted, over what period and from which source.
A page view is not automatically an inquiry. An inquiry is not automatically a customer. Those distinctions help you understand what the work has produced.
Our public results pages link to examples and recorded activity. Read the definitions alongside the numbers.

cta.label: Explore the work and its context

emails.subject: Follow a working example
emails.preheader: Look at the customer path before choosing features.
body: A useful way to review a website is to use it as a customer would.
Choose an example from our portfolio. Look at the offer, the information someone needs and the action they are invited to take.
Then compare that path with your own business. Which parts fit? Which would need to be different?
The point is to identify useful details, not assume another business’s experience predicts your results.

emails.subject: Give follow-up a reason to exist
emails.preheader: Add useful information to the conversation.
body: A follow-up can add something useful.
Answer a question left open. Share the information the person requested. Explain a next step that was unclear.
“Checking in” may fit some situations, but it should not be the only message in your plan. Give the reader a reason to continue the conversation.
Before sending, review the earlier exchange so your message matches what has already happened. If the person declines or opts out, respect that choice.

cta.label: Ask Ryan about a follow-up message

emails.subject: Draft a useful missed-call reply
emails.preheader: Identify the business and set a promise your team can keep.
body: A missed-call message should identify the business and make it easy to respond.
Keep the promise realistic. If the team will reply during business hours, say that. If a particular detail helps route the request, ask for it clearly.
Our free script tool can give you a starting point. Review the wording and use it only where you have permission to contact the recipient.
A written script helps the team; it does not replace judgment.

emails.subject: Turn repeated questions into useful content
emails.preheader: Answer a real question in the customer’s words.
body: Write down the questions your team answers most often.
Choose one and create a plain-language answer for your page or follow-up. Include the detail someone needs to make a decision, and keep any conditions visible.
Schools might explain schedules. Coaches might explain how the first conversation works. Event hosts might explain what happens after registration.
Use the question in the customer’s words. That makes the answer easier to recognize and easier for your team to reuse.

cta.label: Reply with a question you want to answer

emails.subject: Make a handoff someone else can use
emails.preheader: Keep the facts, agreement and next action together.
body: Imagine another team member needs to continue an inquiry tomorrow.
Would the record explain what the person wants, what has been discussed and what should happen next?
A useful note is short and specific. Record the facts, the agreed next step and the responsible person. Avoid making someone reconstruct the entire exchange.
This is one of the practical details we look at when connecting customer records and follow-up.

cta.label: Tell Ryan which handoff needs help

emails.subject: Review what your form asks
emails.preheader: Test where the inquiry goes after someone submits it.
body: Every question on a form should have a purpose.
Read yours and ask how each answer will help the next conversation. Keep necessary questions clear, and explain what happens after submission.
Then submit a test using your own details. Confirm the message reaches the correct place and that the confirmation makes sense.
The useful result is a working handoff. A form can look finished while that part still needs attention.

cta.label: Ask Ryan about your inquiry path

emails.subject: Want the follow-up written for you?
emails.preheader: Review the scope of the $197 writing service.
body: If the main problem is finding the words, our Follow-Up Campaign may fit.
For $197 one time, Ryan writes a set of messages for one offer in your business, including a five-message email sequence and a guide to when the messages belong.
It is a writing service. Sending, advertising, CRM setup and automation implementation are separate.
Review the full scope and intake requirements before purchasing. If you need the connected system, bring that question to the consultation instead.

emails.subject: If the website is the starting point
emails.preheader: Review the five-page Website Launch and payment terms.
body: Sometimes the first useful project is a clearer website with a working inquiry path.
Website Launch is our five-page foundation at $1,000: $500 to start, with the remaining $500 after approval and before launch.
The page explains the included work, review rounds and payment terms. Additional services are scoped separately.
Review those details against what your business needs. If you are unsure whether a website is the right first move, we can discuss that before you decide.

emails.subject: When the pieces need a map
emails.preheader: A written plan can make a larger project easier to assess.
body: If your business relies on several disconnected systems, deciding what to change first can be difficult.
The $497 System Map is a paid planning deliverable. It reviews the current setup, maps the customer path and identifies suggested phases and a price range.
It is separate from the free consultation and from carrying out the build.
Read the scope before choosing it. A clear plan should help you understand the work and its dependencies before committing to a larger project.

emails.subject: Keep your team in the conversation
emails.preheader: Start with the work and the people who use the process.
body: Before changing a workflow, ask the people who use it.
What information do they need? What slows them down? Which part works well already?
The answer may be a clearer task, a better page or a connection between tools. Start with the work itself and choose the tool afterward.
That applies whether your team handles student inquiries, coaching calls, event registrations or community questions. The process needs to make sense to the people using it.

cta.label: Tell Ryan what your team needs

emails.subject: Pick the improvement you can measure
emails.preheader: Choose one change and a useful way to check it.
body: Choose one improvement and decide how you will check it.

If you are changing inquiry routing, confirm the right person receives the information. If you are improving replies, review whether the question gets answered. If you are revising a page, test whether the next step is clear.
Keep the measure close to the change. It is easier to learn when you know what you were trying to improve.

emails.subject: Bring the real business to the call
emails.preheader: A free 30-minute conversation can start with what feels stuck.
body: You do not need a presentation for a consultation with me.
Bring the website, the questions and the part of the process that feels difficult. We can talk about how people find you, where inquiries go and what happens afterward.
The free conversation is 30 minutes. In East Texas, we can meet at your business or the Longview office; phone and video are also options.
Reply with what you want to work through, or request the consultation on the site.

emails.subject: Which next step fits your business?
emails.preheader: The last message in your 30-day series.
body: This is the last email in the 30-day series.
You have looked at the offer, website, inquiries, follow-up and the work behind your customer conversations. Which part deserves your attention now?
You can keep using the free tools, choose a defined service or talk with me about the next step.
There is no deadline attached to this message. If you want help, reply with the problem you want to work through.
Thanks for spending some of your time with The LeadFlow Pro.
